claim: Meta-analyses are increasingly used for synthesis of evidence from biomedical research.
source: Meta-analyses are increasingly used for synthesis of evidence from biomedical research, and often include an assessment of publication bias based on visual or analytical detection of asymmetry in funnel plots.
evidence: This is a general statement about the increasing use of meta-analyses in biomedical research, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Meta-analyses often include an assessment of publication bias based on visual or analytical detection of asymmetry in funnel plots.
source: Meta-analyses are increasingly used for synthesis of evidence from biomedical research, and often include an assessment of publication bias based on visual or analytical detection of asymmetry in funnel plots.
evidence: This describes a common practice in meta-analysis methodology, based on established knowledge.

claim: Funnel plots of the Standardized Mean Difference (SMD) plotted against the standard error (SE) are susceptible to distortion.
source: We found that funnel plots of the Standardized Mean Difference (SMD) plotted against the standard error (SE) are susceptible to distortion, leading to overestimation of the existence and extent of publication bias.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's empirical datasets and simulations.

claim: SMD vs. SE funnel plots lead to overestimation of the existence and extent of publication bias.
source: We found that funnel plots of the Standardized Mean Difference (SMD) plotted against the standard error (SE) are susceptible to distortion, leading to overestimation of the existence and extent of publication bias.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Distortion in SMD vs. SE funnel plots was more severe when the primary studies had a small sample size.
source: Distortion was more severe when the primary studies had a small sample size and when an intervention effect was present.
evidence: This finding is supported by the simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Distortion in SMD vs. SE funnel plots was more severe when an intervention effect was present.
source: Distortion was more severe when the primary studies had a small sample size and when an intervention effect was present.
evidence: This finding is supported by the simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Using the Normalised Mean Difference measure as effect size is a more reliable alternative to SMD for publication bias assessment.
source: We show that using the Normalised Mean Difference measure as effect size (when possible), or plotting the SMD against a sample size-based precision estimate, are more reliable alternatives.
evidence: This recommendation is based on the simulation and empirical data analysis presented in the study.

claim: Plotting the SMD against a sample size-based precision estimate is a more reliable alternative to SMD vs. SE funnel plots.
source: We show that using the Normalised Mean Difference measure as effect size (when possible), or plotting the SMD against a sample size-based precision estimate, are more reliable alternatives.
evidence: This recommendation is based on the simulation and empirical data analysis presented in the study.

claim: Funnel plots using the SMD in combination with the SE are unsuitable for publication bias assessments.
source: We conclude that funnel plots using the SMD in combination with the SE are unsuitable for publication bias assessments and can lead to false-positive results.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the presented data and simulations.

claim: SMD vs. SE funnel plots can lead to false-positive results in publication bias assessments.
source: We conclude that funnel plots using the SMD in combination with the SE are unsuitable for publication bias assessments and can lead to false-positive results.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the simulation results showing asymmetry detection in unbiased datasets.

claim: Published research is more likely to have positive or statistically significant results than unpublished experiments.
source: Simultaneously, meta-analysis can be used to assess the risk of publication bias: the phenomenon that published research is more likely to have positive or statistically significant results than unpublished experiments (Dwan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a definition of publication bias supported by a citation to Dwan et al., 2013.

claim: Meta-analyses are routinely used in clinical research to guide clinical practice and healthcare policy.
source: Meta-analyses are routinely used in clinical research to guide clinical practice and healthcare policy, reduce research waste and increase patient safety (Chalmers et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chalmers et al., 2014.

claim: Meta-analyses are used to reduce research waste and increase patient safety.
source: Meta-analyses are routinely used in clinical research to guide clinical practice and healthcare policy, reduce research waste and increase patient safety (Chalmers et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chalmers et al., 2014.

claim: The use of meta-analysis continues to increase.
source: The use of meta-analysis continues to increase (Bastian et al., 2010) and it has become more common to apply these approaches to the synthesis of preclinical evidence (Korevaar et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bastian et al., 2010.

claim: It has become more common to apply meta-analysis approaches to the synthesis of preclinical evidence.
source: The use of meta-analysis continues to increase (Bastian et al., 2010) and it has become more common to apply these approaches to the synthesis of preclinical evidence (Korevaar et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Korevaar et al., 2011.

claim: Preclinical studies are generally individually small.
source: Importantly, preclinical studies are, generally, individually small, with large numbers of studies included in meta-analysis, and large observed effects of interventions.
evidence: This is a general characterization of preclinical studies based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Preclinical meta-analyses typically include large numbers of studies.
source: Importantly, preclinical studies are, generally, individually small, with large numbers of studies included in meta-analysis, and large observed effects of interventions.
evidence: This is a general characterization of preclinical meta-analyses based on established knowledge.

claim: Preclinical studies typically show large observed effects of interventions.
source: Importantly, preclinical studies are, generally, individually small, with large numbers of studies included in meta-analysis, and large observed effects of interventions.
evidence: This is a general characterization of preclinical studies based on established knowledge.

claim: Clinical meta-analyses usually involve a smaller number of individually larger experiments with smaller intervention effects compared to preclinical meta-analyses.
source: This contrasts with clinical research, where meta-analyses usually involve a smaller number of individually larger experiments with smaller intervention effects.
evidence: This is a general characterization of clinical meta-analyses based on established knowledge.

claim: The RMD can be used when all outcome data are in the same measurement unit.
source: The RMD can be used when all outcome data are in the same measurement unit, and the interpretation of the outcome is the same in all settings (i.e. the reported measurement unit of the change in outcome has the same meaning in all studies).
evidence: This is a methodological definition based on established statistical knowledge.

claim: The RMD can be used when the interpretation of the outcome is the same in all settings.
source: The RMD can be used when all outcome data are in the same measurement unit, and the interpretation of the outcome is the same in all settings (i.e. the reported measurement unit of the change in outcome has the same meaning in all studies).
evidence: This is a methodological definition based on established statistical knowledge.

claim: The RMD is calculated by subtracting the mean outcome value in the control group from the mean in the intervention group.
source: The RMD is calculated by subtracting the mean outcome value in the control group (Mctrl) from the mean in the intervention group (Mint):
evidence: This is a mathematical definition of the RMD calculation.

claim: The observed standard deviation is likely to differ between experimental groups.
source: The observed standard deviation (SD) is likely to differ between experimental groups, and therefore the standard error (SE) of the RMD is calculated as:
evidence: This is a general statistical observation based on established knowledge.

claim: The intervention effect may be expressed as an SMD when the measurement unit or the interpretation of the outcome differ between studies.
source: In cases where the measurement unit, or the interpretation of the outcome, or both differ between studies (e.g. a given change in infarct size measured in mm3 has a different consequence in the mouse brain than in the rat brain), the intervention effect may be expressed as an SMD.
evidence: This is a methodological explanation based on established statistical knowledge.

claim: The SMD expresses the intervention effect in all studies in the same new unit: the SD.
source: Thus, the SMD expresses the intervention effect in all studies in the same new unit: the SD.
evidence: This is a methodological explanation of what the SMD represents.

claim: Cohen's d tends to overestimate the 'true' SMD and its variance when the sample sizes in the primary studies are small.
source: However, Cohen's d tends to overestimate the 'true' SMD and its variance when the sample sizes in the primary studies are small (e.g. <10).
evidence: This is a known property of Cohen's d based on established statistical knowledge.

claim: Hedges' g adjusts both the SMD estimate and its variance by a correction factor based on the total sample size.
source: This bias can be corrected using the approach of Hedges (Hedges, 1981), which adjusts both the SMD estimate and its variance by a correction factor based on the total sample size.
evidence: This is a methodological explanation supported by a citation to Hedges, 1981.

claim: In many clinical meta-analyses, Hedges' g will be almost identical to Cohen's d.
source: In many clinical meta-analyses, Hedges' g will be almost identical to Cohen's d, but the difference between the estimates can be larger in preclinical meta-analyses, where small sample sizes are more common.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the two estimators and typical sample sizes in clinical studies.

claim: The difference between Hedges' g and Cohen's d can be larger in preclinical meta-analyses, where small sample sizes are more common.
source: In many clinical meta-analyses, Hedges' g will be almost identical to Cohen's d, but the difference between the estimates can be larger in preclinical meta-analyses, where small sample sizes are more common.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the two estimators and typical sample sizes in preclinical studies.

claim: A condition for using the NMD is that the baseline measurement in an untreated, unlesioned 'sham' animal is known, or can be inferred.
source: A condition for using the NMD is that the baseline measurement in an untreated, unlesioned 'sham' animal is known, or can be inferred.
evidence: This is a methodological requirement for using the NMD, based on the definition provided by Vesterinen et al., 2014.

claim: The SESMD is correlated to the SMD effect size.
source: Note that Equation 5 dictates that the SESMD is correlated to the SMD effect size, whereas the SEs of the RMD (Equation 2) and NMD (Equation 7) are independent of the corresponding effect sizes.
evidence: This is a mathematical observation derived from Equation 5.

claim: The SEs of the RMD and NMD are independent of the corresponding effect sizes.
source: Note that Equation 5 dictates that the SESMD is correlated to the SMD effect size, whereas the SEs of the RMD (Equation 2) and NMD (Equation 7) are independent of the corresponding effect sizes.
evidence: This is a mathematical observation derived from Equations 2 and 7.

claim: In the absence of bias and heterogeneity, funnel plots should be funnel-shaped and symmetrically centred around the summary effect estimate.
source: In the absence of bias and heterogeneity, funnel plots should be funnel-shaped and symmetrically centred around the summary effect estimate of the analysis, since 1) imprecise (smaller) studies will deviate further from the summary effect compared to precise (larger) studies and 2) studies are equally likely to overestimate or underestimate the true effect (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation based on statistical principles, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Imprecise (smaller) studies will deviate further from the summary effect compared to precise (larger) studies.
source: In the absence of bias and heterogeneity, funnel plots should be funnel-shaped and symmetrically centred around the summary effect estimate of the analysis, since 1) imprecise (smaller) studies will deviate further from the summary effect compared to precise (larger) studies and 2) studies are equally likely to overestimate or underestimate the true effect (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a statistical principle explaining the funnel shape.

claim: Studies are equally likely to overestimate or underestimate the true effect in the absence of bias.
source: In the absence of bias and heterogeneity, funnel plots should be funnel-shaped and symmetrically centred around the summary effect estimate of the analysis, since 1) imprecise (smaller) studies will deviate further from the summary effect compared to precise (larger) studies and 2) studies are equally likely to overestimate or underestimate the true effect (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a statistical principle explaining funnel plot symmetry.

claim: If studies showing small, neutral or controversial effects are more likely to remain unpublished, publication bias may occur.
source: If studies showing small, neutral or controversial effects are more likely to remain unpublished, publication bias may occur.
evidence: This is a definition of how publication bias arises, based on established knowledge.

claim: Publication bias causes the funnel plot to become asymmetrical.
source: As a result, the funnel plot will become asymmetrical, and the summary effect estimate will shift accordingly (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a consequence of publication bias, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Publication bias causes the summary effect estimate to shift.
source: As a result, the funnel plot will become asymmetrical, and the summary effect estimate will shift accordingly (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a consequence of publication bias, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: There are other causes of asymmetry in funnel plots besides publication bias.
source: Importantly, there are other causes of asymmetry in funnel plots.
evidence: This is a general statement about funnel plot interpretation based on established knowledge.

claim: The true effect size in smaller studies may be genuinely different from that in large studies.
source: For instance, the true effect size in smaller (and therefore less precise) studies may be genuinely different from that in large studies (for instance because the intensity of the intervention was higher in small studies).
evidence: This is an example of an alternative explanation for funnel plot asymmetry.

claim: Funnel plot asymmetry is often referred to as a method to detect small study effects, rather than being a definitive test for publication bias.
source: For this reason, funnel plot asymmetry is often referred to as a method to detect small study effects, rather than being a definitive test for publication bias (Rothstein et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a clarification about the interpretation of funnel plot asymmetry, supported by a citation to Rothstein et al., 2005.

claim: Artefacts and chance may cause asymmetry in funnel plots.
source: In addition, artefacts and chance may cause asymmetry (as shown e.g. in this study).
evidence: This statement is supported by the findings of the current study.

claim: If there is no intervention effect, the SMD will be zero, and the SE will depend solely on the sample size.
source: If there is no intervention effect, the SMD (and the second component) will be zero, and the SE will therefore depend solely on the sample size (Equation 5 and Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a mathematical consequence of Equation 5, illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: If an intervention effect is present, the SE of the SMD will increase, as the size of SMD2 in the equation will increase.
source: If an intervention effect is present, the SE will increase, as the size of SMD2 in the equation will increase.
evidence: This is a mathematical consequence of Equation 5.

claim: A study with an observed SMD larger than the true SMD will have a larger SE.
source: However, a study with an observed SMD larger than the true SMD will have a larger SE.
evidence: This is a mathematical consequence of the relationship between SMD and SE in Equation 5.

claim: A study with an observed SMD smaller than the true SMD (but >0) will have a relatively small SE.
source: On the other hand, a study with an observed SMD smaller than the true SMD (but >0) will have a relatively small SE (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a mathematical consequence of the relationship between SMD and SE, illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: Studies with a relatively small effect size will skew towards the upper left region of the SMD vs. SE funnel plot.
source: This will cause funnel plot distortion: studies with a relatively small effect size (and associated SE) will skew towards the upper left region of the plot, while studies with a relatively large effect size and SE will skew towards the bottom right region of the plot, as the associated SE of these studies will be relatively large.
evidence: This is a consequence of the mathematical relationship between SMD and SE.

claim: Studies with a relatively large effect size will skew towards the bottom right region of the SMD vs. SE funnel plot.
source: This will cause funnel plot distortion: studies with a relatively small effect size (and associated SE) will skew towards the upper left region of the plot, while studies with a relatively large effect size and SE will skew towards the bottom right region of the plot, as the associated SE of these studies will be relatively large.
evidence: This is a consequence of the mathematical relationship between SMD and SE.

claim: The distortion pattern in SMD vs. SE funnel plots holds true for both positive and negative SMDs because the SMD is squared in the equation for the SE.
source: Because the SMD is squared in the equation for the SE, this holds true for both positive and negative SMDs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a mathematical consequence illustrated in Figure 2C.

claim: The smaller the first component of Equation 5, the larger the influence of the SMD on the size of the SE.
source: The smaller the first component of Equation 5, the larger the influence of the SMD on the size of the SE, worsening the distortion when sample sizes are small.
evidence: This is a mathematical observation from Equation 5.

claim: The first component of Equation 5 is smallest when group sizes are unequal.
source: Of note, this component is smallest when group sizes are unequal.
evidence: This is a mathematical observation from Equation 5.

claim: The effect of the second component on the SE is largest if the sample size is small and the SMD is large.
source: The effect of the second component on the SE, and the resulting distortion, is largest if the sample size is small and the SMD is large (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a mathematical observation illustrated in Figure 2D.

claim: A funnel plot using both the SMD and its SE may become asymmetrical in the absence of publication bias.
source: In summary, a funnel plot using both the SMD and its SE may become asymmetrical in the absence of publication bias.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the theoretical explanation provided.

claim: Funnel plot distortion might cause the plot to be interpreted as being asymmetrical and lead the observer to erroneously conclude that publication bias is present.
source: When funnel plot distortion is assessed by visual inspection, this skewing might cause the plot to be interpreted as being asymmetrical and lead the observer to erroneously conclude that publication bias is present.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the distortion phenomenon.

claim: Egger's regression and Duval and Tweedie's trim and fill analysis do not take the SMD-SE correlation phenomenon into account.
source: Furthermore, funnel plot asymmetry is often tested statistically using Egger's regression (Egger et al., 1997) or Duval and Tweedie's trim and fill analysis (Duval and Tweedie, 2000), but neither of these analyses take the phenomenon described above into account, and their use may lead to erroneous conclusions that publication bias is present.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of these statistical methods in the context of SMD vs. SE funnel plots.

claim: The use of Egger's regression or trim and fill analysis on SMD vs. SE funnel plots may lead to erroneous conclusions that publication bias is present.
source: Furthermore, funnel plot asymmetry is often tested statistically using Egger's regression (Egger et al., 1997) or Duval and Tweedie's trim and fill analysis (Duval and Tweedie, 2000), but neither of these analyses take the phenomenon described above into account, and their use may lead to erroneous conclusions that publication bias is present.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the theoretical analysis and supported by the simulation results.

claim: Dataset 1 (ischaemic preconditioning) contains 785 individual effect sizes.
source: Dataset 1 (ischaemic preconditioning) contains 785 individual effect sizes (Wever et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the empirical dataset used in the study.

claim: In Dataset 1, funnel plot asymmetry was detected by Egger's regression (p=1.7×10−5) when using RMD.
source: In the original analysis using the RMD as effect measure, funnel plot asymmetry was detected by Egger's regression (p=1.7×10−5), but no additional studies were imputed in trim and fill analysis (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from the re-analysis of Dataset 1.

claim: In Dataset 1, no additional studies were imputed in trim and fill analysis when using RMD.
source: In the original analysis using the RMD as effect measure, funnel plot asymmetry was detected by Egger's regression (p=1.7×10−5), but no additional studies were imputed in trim and fill analysis (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from the re-analysis of Dataset 1.

claim: When expressing Dataset 1 as SMD, funnel plot asymmetry increased substantially (p<1.0×10−15).
source: When expressing the same data as SMD, funnel plot asymmetry increased substantially (Figure 3B; p<1.0×10−15, Egger regression) and 196 missing studies were imputed by trim and fill analysis, leading to adjustment of the estimated SMD effect size from 2.8 to 1.9.
evidence: This is a result from the re-analysis of Dataset 1.

claim: In Dataset 1 expressed as SMD, 196 missing studies were imputed by trim and fill analysis.
source: When expressing the same data as SMD, funnel plot asymmetry increased substantially (Figure 3B; p<1.0×10−15, Egger regression) and 196 missing studies were imputed by trim and fill analysis, leading to adjustment of the estimated SMD effect size from 2.8 to 1.9.
evidence: This is a result from the re-analysis of Dataset 1.

claim: In Dataset 1 expressed as SMD, the estimated effect size was adjusted from 2.8 to 1.9 after trim and fill analysis.
source: When expressing the same data as SMD, funnel plot asymmetry increased substantially (Figure 3B; p<1.0×10−15, Egger regression) and 196 missing studies were imputed by trim and fill analysis, leading to adjustment of the estimated SMD effect size from 2.8 to 1.9.
evidence: This is a result from the re-analysis of Dataset 1.

claim: Dataset 2 (stem cell treatments) contained 95 individual effect sizes.
source: Dataset 2 (stem cell treatments) contained 95 individual effect sizes (Zwetsloot et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the empirical dataset used in the study.

claim: In Dataset 2, funnel plot asymmetry was detected in the original analysis using RMD (p=0.02).
source: Funnel plot asymmetry was detected in the original analysis using RMD (p=0.02) and trim and fill analysis suggested a reduction in effect estimate of 0.1% after filling two additional studies (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a result from the re-analysis of Dataset 2.

claim: In Dataset 2 using RMD, trim and fill analysis suggested a reduction in effect estimate of 0.1% after filling two additional studies.
source: Funnel plot asymmetry was detected in the original analysis using RMD (p=0.02) and trim and fill analysis suggested a reduction in effect estimate of 0.1% after filling two additional studies (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a result from the re-analysis of Dataset 2.

claim: In Dataset 2 expressed as SMD, funnel plot asymmetry was detected at a higher level of statistical significance (p=3.4×10−10).
source: In contrast, a funnel plot of the same data expressed as SMD showed asymmetry at a higher level of statistical significance (p=3.4×10−10, Egger regression), but no missing studies were imputed (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a result from the re-analysis of Dataset 2.

claim: In Dataset 2 expressed as SMD, no missing studies were imputed by trim and fill analysis.
source: In contrast, a funnel plot of the same data expressed as SMD showed asymmetry at a higher level of statistical significance (p=3.4×10−10, Egger regression), but no missing studies were imputed (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a result from the re-analysis of Dataset 2.

claim: When no intervention effect was simulated, neither Egger's regression nor trim and fill analysis gave different results for the RMD vs. SE and SMD vs. SE analyses.
source: When we simulated no intervention effect, neither Egger's regression nor trim and fill analysis gave different results for the RMD vs. SE and SMD vs. SE analyses (Table 1, Figure 4A,B,E and F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, panel A, B, E and F) and in ~95% of cases there was no evidence of asymmetry.
evidence: This is a result from simulation 1.

claim: In simulations with no intervention effect, in ~95% of cases there was no evidence of asymmetry.
source: When we simulated no intervention effect, neither Egger's regression nor trim and fill analysis gave different results for the RMD vs. SE and SMD vs. SE analyses (Table 1, Figure 4A,B,E and F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, panel A, B, E and F) and in ~95% of cases there was no evidence of asymmetry.
evidence: This is a result from simulation 1.

claim: Around 5% of simulated funnel plots with no intervention effect were assessed as asymmetrical by chance.
source: Most simulated funnel plots were assessed as symmetrical, however, as expected, around 5% of the cases were considered asymmetrical by chance.
evidence: This is a result from simulation 1, consistent with the expected false positive rate at p<0.05.

claim: When using the SMD with an intervention effect present, funnel plot asymmetry was detected in over 60% of the simulated funnel plots with Δμ = 10 and small study sizes.
source: In contrast, when using the SMD, funnel plot asymmetry was detected in over 60% of the simulated funnel plots with Δμ = 10, where the size of contributing studies was small (Figure 4D and H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, panel D and H), increasing as the number of individual studies contributing to the meta-analysis increased.
evidence: This is a result from simulation 1.

claim: The percentage of SMD funnel plots assessed as asymmetrical increased as the number of individual studies contributing to the meta-analysis increased.
source: In contrast, when using the SMD, funnel plot asymmetry was detected in over 60% of the simulated funnel plots with Δμ = 10, where the size of contributing studies was small (Figure 4D and H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, panel D and H), increasing as the number of individual studies contributing to the meta-analysis increased.
evidence: This is a result from simulation 1.

claim: When individual studies were larger (n = 60–320 subjects), respectively 9%, 34% and 100% of the SMD funnel plots with 30, 300 or 3000 studies were assessed as asymmetrical.
source: When we modelled larger individual contributing studies (n = 60–320 subjects), respectively 9%, 34% and 100% of the SMD funnel plots with 30, 300 or 3000 studies were assessed as asymmetrical (Table 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from simulation 1.

claim: Trim and fill analysis resulted in on average 7% extra studies filled in preclinical simulation scenarios using the RMD.
source: Trim and fill analysis resulted in on average 7% extra studies filled in preclinical simulation scenarios using the RMD.
evidence: This is a result from simulation 1.

claim: Adjusting the overall effect estimate based on trim and fill filled data points improved the estimation of the simulated RMD in all scenarios.
source: Adjusting the overall effect estimate based on these filled data points improved the estimation of the simulated RMD in all scenarios.
evidence: This is a result from simulation 1.

claim: When using the SMD, the number of filled studies in trim and fill analysis was much higher in many scenarios (up to 21% extra studies filled).
source: However, when using the SMD, the number of filled studies was much higher in many scenarios (up to 21% extra studies filled).
evidence: This is a result from simulation 1.

claim: The adjusted overall effect estimate after trim and fill in SMD funnel plots tended to be an underestimation of the true effect size.
source: As a result, the adjusted overall effect estimate after trim and fill in SMD funnel plots tended to be an underestimation of the true effect size.
evidence: This is a result from simulation 1.

claim: Distortion could be seen in all SMD funnel plots that incorporated a true effect, most prominent in the preclinical (small study) scenarios.
source: Finally, through visual inspection, distortion could be seen in all SMD funnel plots that incorporated a true effect, most prominent in the preclinical (small study) scenarios (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from visual inspection of simulation 1 funnel plots.

claim: When repeating the simulations using Cohen's d SMD instead of Hedges' g, highly similar results were found in all scenarios simulated.
source: When repeating the simulations using Cohen's d SMD instead of Hedges' g, or using Begg and Mazumdar's test, we found highly similar results in all scenarios simulated (see Supplementary file 1 and exemplary funnel plots in Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from the sensitivity analysis.

claim: When using Begg and Mazumdar's test, highly similar results were found in all scenarios simulated.
source: When repeating the simulations using Cohen's d SMD instead of Hedges' g, or using Begg and Mazumdar's test, we found highly similar results in all scenarios simulated (see Supplementary file 1 and exemplary funnel plots in Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from the sensitivity analysis.

claim: SMD vs. SE funnel plots of unbiased simulations were identified as asymmetrical by Egger's test.
source: As in simulation 1, SMD vs. SE funnel plots of unbiased simulations were identified as asymmetrical by Egger's test (Table 2).
evidence: This is a result from simulation 2.

claim: When the precision estimate was changed from SE to 1/√n, the prevalence of false positive results fell to the expected 5%.
source: However, when the precision estimate was changed from SE to 1/√n, the prevalence of false positive results fell to the expected 5% (Table 2).
evidence: This is a result from simulation 2.

claim: For the NMD, Egger's test performed correctly when using either the SE or 1/√n as precision estimate.
source: For the NMD, Egger's test performed correctly when using either the SE or 1/√n as precision estimate.
evidence: This is a result from simulation 2.

claim: In all scenarios of simulation 2, approximately 50 out of 1000 simulated funnel plots appeared to be asymmetrical by chance.
source: In all scenario's, approximately 50 out of 1000 simulated funnel plots appeared to be asymmetrical by chance (Table 2).
evidence: This is a result from simulation 2.

claim: The typical left-upward shift of the small SMD datapoints and right-downward shift of the large SMD data points is clearly visible in the SMD vs. SE plot.
source: The typical left-upward shift of the small SMD datapoints and right-downward shift of the large SMD data points is clearly visible in the SMD vs. SE plot (Figure 5B), but not in the RMD, SMD vs. 1/√n or NMD plots.
evidence: This is an observation from visual inspection of Figure 5B.

claim: The distortion pattern is not visible in the RMD, SMD vs. 1/√n or NMD plots.
source: The typical left-upward shift of the small SMD datapoints and right-downward shift of the large SMD data points is clearly visible in the SMD vs. SE plot (Figure 5B), but not in the RMD, SMD vs. 1/√n or NMD plots.
evidence: This is an observation from visual inspection of Figure 5.

claim: SMD vs.1/√n funnel plots performed as well as the RMD vs. SE funnel plots in both biased and unbiased simulations when the size of individual studies was small.
source: When the size of individual studies was small, SMD vs.1/√n funnel plots performed as well as the RMD vs. SE funnel plots, in both biased and unbiased simulations (Table 2).
evidence: This is a result from simulation 3.

claim: The NMD behaved similar to the RMD with either an SE or 1/√n precision estimate.
source: The NMD also behaved similar to the RMD with either an SE or 1/√n precision estimate.
evidence: This is a result from simulation 3.

claim: In three out of five re-analyzed published meta-analyses, asymmetry detected with SMD vs. SE was not present in funnel plots using 1/√n as a precision estimate.
source: In the original publications, all five of these funnel plots were asymmetrical according to Egger's regression test. In three out of five cases, this asymmetry was not present in funnel plots using 1/√n as a precision estimate (Table 3 and Figure 7).
evidence: This is a result from the re-analysis of published meta-analyses.

claim: Missing data points detected by trim and fill analysis in three out of five published papers were not detected when using SMD vs. 1/√n funnel plots.
source: Furthermore, three out of five papers reported several missing data points, as detected by trim and fill analysis. Missing data points were not detected when using SMD vs. 1/√n funnel plots for trim and fill analysis (Table 3 and Figure 7).
evidence: This is a result from the re-analysis of published meta-analyses.

claim: The use of Egger's regression test for funnel plot asymmetry based on plotting SMD against SE is associated with substantial over-estimation of asymmetry.
source: Using data from both simulated and empirical meta-analyses, we have shown that the use of Egger's regression test for funnel plot asymmetry based on plotting SMD against SE is associated with such a substantial over-estimation of asymmetry as to render this approach of little value, particularly when the size of contributing studies is small.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on the presented data.

claim: SMD vs. SE funnel plots are of little value for publication bias assessment, particularly when the size of contributing studies is small.
source: Using data from both simulated and empirical meta-analyses, we have shown that the use of Egger's regression test for funnel plot asymmetry based on plotting SMD against SE is associated with such a substantial over-estimation of asymmetry as to render this approach of little value, particularly when the size of contributing studies is small.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on the presented data.

claim: Distortion in SMD vs. SE funnel plots occurs whenever an intervention effect is present, in meta-analyses both with and without publication bias.
source: This distortion occurs whenever an intervention effect is present, in meta-analyses both with and without publication bias.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation results.

claim: The severity of distortion and the risk of misinterpretation are influenced by the sample size of the individual studies, the number of studies in the meta-analysis, and the presence or absence of an intervention effect.
source: The severity of distortion and the risk of misinterpretation are influenced by the sample size of the individual studies, the number of studies in the meta-analysis, and the presence or absence of an intervention effect.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation results.

claim: The use of SMD vs. SE funnel plots may lead to invalid conclusions about the presence or absence of publication bias and should not be used.
source: Thus, the use of SMD vs. SE funnel plots may lead to invalid conclusions about the presence or absence of publication bias and should not be used.
evidence: This is a main recommendation of the study based on the presented data.

claim: It is almost inevitable that the issues described will occur with any test for publication bias that relies on an assessment of funnel plot asymmetry when using SMD vs. SE.
source: Since it is the association between the SMD and its SE that leads to funnel plot distortion, it almost inevitable that the issues described will occur with any test for publication bias that relies on an assessment of funnel plot asymmetry (e.g. Begg and Mazumdar's test [Begg and Mazumdar, 1994]).
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of distortion and supported by the sensitivity analysis using Begg and Mazumdar's test.

claim: When using trim and fill analysis on SMD vs. SE funnel plots, funnel plot distortion introduces the risk of incorrectly adjusting the summary effect estimate.
source: When using trim and fill analysis, funnel plot distortion introduces the risk of incorrectly adjusting the summary effect estimate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation results showing underestimation of effect sizes after trim and fill.

claim: Previous reports of the presence of publication bias based on SMD vs. SE funnel plots should be re-evaluated, both for pre-clinical and clinical meta-analyses.
source: Previous reports of the presence of publication bias based on this approach should be re-evaluated, both for pre-clinical and clinical meta-analyses.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Distortion does not occur in NMD vs. SE funnel plots.
source: Importantly, distortion does not occur in NMD vs. SE funnel plots, which formed the basis of a recent analysis showing evidence for substantial publication bias in the animal stroke literature (Sena et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation results and supported by citation to Sena et al., 2010.

claim: A similar phenomenon to SMD funnel plot distortion has been reported for the use of odds ratios in funnel plots.
source: A similar phenomenon has been reported for the use of odds ratios in funnel plots, which also induces artificial significant results in Egger's regression (Peters et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Peters et al., 2006.

claim: An alternative test based on sample size has been proposed for odds ratios to circumvent the problem of funnel plot distortion.
source: Here, too, an alternative test based on sample size has been proposed to circumvent this problem (Peters et al., 2006), and we suggest to extend this recommendation to SMDs.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Peters et al., 2006.

claim: The authors suggest extending the recommendation to use sample size-based precision estimates to SMDs.
source: Here, too, an alternative test based on sample size has been proposed to circumvent this problem (Peters et al., 2006), and we suggest to extend this recommendation to SMDs.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: The RMD approach is limited because there are many instances where a given change may have very different biological importance even when the same units of measurement are used.
source: The RMD approach is limited because there are many instances (for example across species) where, although the same units of measurement are used, a given change may have very different biological importance.
evidence: This is a discussion of the limitations of the RMD approach based on established knowledge.

claim: The NMD approach is preferred over SMD.
source: The NMD approach is preferred, but – because it expresses the effects of an intervention as a proportion of lesion size – there may be circumstances where outcome in a non-lesioned animal is not reported or cannot be inferred, and here the NMD approach is not possible.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: There may be circumstances where outcome in a non-lesioned animal is not reported or cannot be inferred, making the NMD approach not possible.
source: The NMD approach is preferred, but – because it expresses the effects of an intervention as a proportion of lesion size – there may be circumstances where outcome in a non-lesioned animal is not reported or cannot be inferred, and here the NMD approach is not possible.
evidence: This is a discussion of the limitations of the NMD approach.

claim: The relative performance of RMD, NMD and SMD approaches in identifying heterogeneity between groups of animal studies or in meta-regression is not known.
source: Further, the relative performance of RMD, NMD and SMD approaches in identifying heterogeneity between groups of animal studies (partitioning of heterogeneity) or in meta-regression is not known.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a knowledge gap.

claim: The findings may be especially relevant for preclinical meta-analyses because of the increased distortion seen when contributing studies are individually small.
source: Taken with the increased distortion seen when contributing studies are individually small, this means our findings may be especially relevant for preclinical meta-analyses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the simulation results and characteristics of preclinical studies.

claim: The SMD is frequently used in preclinical meta-analyses to overcome expected heterogeneity between data obtained from different animal species.
source: The SMD is frequently used in preclinical meta-analyses to overcome expected heterogeneity between data obtained from different animal species.
evidence: This is a statement about current practice in preclinical meta-analyses.

claim: The SMD is also used in clinical meta-analyses.
source: Nevertheless, the SMD is also used in clinical meta-analyses and the degree of distortion cannot be readily predicted.
evidence: This is a statement about current practice in clinical meta-analyses.

claim: The degree of distortion in clinical meta-analyses using SMD vs. SE funnel plots cannot be readily predicted.
source: Nevertheless, the SMD is also used in clinical meta-analyses and the degree of distortion cannot be readily predicted.
evidence: This is an inference based on the variability in clinical study characteristics.

claim: Distortion causes the threshold for determining publication bias to be artificially lowered when using SMDs and their SE.
source: In any case, distortion causes the threshold for determining publication bias to be artificially lowered when using SMDs and their SE, increasing the chance of false-positive results.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation results.

claim: Distortion in SMD vs. SE funnel plots increases the chance of false-positive results in publication bias assessment.
source: In any case, distortion causes the threshold for determining publication bias to be artificially lowered when using SMDs and their SE, increasing the chance of false-positive results.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation results.

claim: Trim and fill analysis may not always be reliable when the number of studies in a meta-analysis is large.
source: Of note, trim and fill analysis may not always be reliable when the number of studies in a meta-analysis is large; in half of the cases of our unbiased simulations with 300 and 3000 studies, many studies were deemed missing, even if no intervention effect was introduced.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation results.

claim: In unbiased simulations with 300 and 3000 studies, many studies were deemed missing by trim and fill analysis in half of the cases, even if no intervention effect was introduced.
source: Of note, trim and fill analysis may not always be reliable when the number of studies in a meta-analysis is large; in half of the cases of our unbiased simulations with 300 and 3000 studies, many studies were deemed missing, even if no intervention effect was introduced.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation results.

claim: The SMD simulations were always more susceptible to the addition of imputed studies if a true effect was introduced.
source: Still, the SMD simulations were always more susceptible to the addition of imputed studies if a true effect was introduced, and the effect size reduction was larger compared to RMD measurements.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation results.

claim: The effect size reduction after trim and fill was larger for SMD compared to RMD measurements.
source: Still, the SMD simulations were always more susceptible to the addition of imputed studies if a true effect was introduced, and the effect size reduction was larger compared to RMD measurements.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation results.

claim: The authors recommend that investigators use RMD or NMD instead of SMD when seeking evidence of publication bias in meta-analyses, where possible.
source: We recommend that, where possible, investigators use RMD or NMD instead of SMD when seeking evidence of publication bias in meta-analyses.
evidence: This is a main recommendation of the study.

claim: Where it is necessary to use SMD, assessment for publication bias should use a sample size-based precision estimate such as 1/√n.
source: Where it is necessary to use SMD, assessment for publication bias should use a sample size-based precision estimate such as 1/√n.
evidence: This is a main recommendation of the study based on the simulation results.

claim: In a given analysis it may be possible to calculate an NMD effect size for some but not all studies.
source: In a given analysis it may be possible to calculate an NMD effect size for some but not all studies.
evidence: This is a practical consideration for applying the NMD approach.

claim: There is a trade-off between the reduced number of included studies and an improved estimation of publication bias when using NMD for only some studies.
source: In these circumstances there is a trade-off between the reduced number of included studies and an improved estimation of publication bias, and sensitivity analysis may be used to compare the meta-analysis outcome using the NMD versus the SMD.
evidence: This is a practical consideration for applying the NMD approach.

claim: Sensitivity analysis may be used to compare the meta-analysis outcome using the NMD versus the SMD.
source: In these circumstances there is a trade-off between the reduced number of included studies and an improved estimation of publication bias, and sensitivity analysis may be used to compare the meta-analysis outcome using the NMD versus the SMD.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation.

claim: Other methods to investigate publication bias in a dataset may be used in addition to funnel plots.
source: Of note, other methods to investigate publication bias in a dataset may be used in addition to funnel plots (e.g. fail-safe N, Excess Significance Test [Ioannidis and Trikalinos, 2007], or selection method / weight funcion model approaches [Peters et al., 2006]), but the performance of these approaches in the context of SMD, RMD and NMD estimates of effect size is not known.
evidence: This is a statement about alternative methods supported by citations.

claim: The performance of alternative publication bias detection methods in the context of SMD, RMD and NMD estimates of effect size is not known.
source: Of note, other methods to investigate publication bias in a dataset may be used in addition to funnel plots (e.g. fail-safe N, Excess Significance Test [Ioannidis and Trikalinos, 2007], or selection method / weight funcion model approaches [Peters et al., 2006]), but the performance of these approaches in the context of SMD, RMD and NMD estimates of effect size is not known.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a knowledge gap.

claim: Funnel plots based on SMDs and their SE should be interpreted with caution.
source: In conclusion, funnel plots based on SMDs and their SE should be interpreted with caution, as the chosen precision estimate is crucial for detection of real funnel plot asymmetry.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The chosen precision estimate is crucial for detection of real funnel plot asymmetry.
source: In conclusion, funnel plots based on SMDs and their SE should be interpreted with caution, as the chosen precision estimate is crucial for detection of real funnel plot asymmetry.
